summary.text: For \(n=14\), the prime counts in the successive intervals \(((k-1)14,k14]\) are \(6,3,4,3,3,4,2,4,1,4,2,3,3,2\), so adjacent counts agree only for \(k=4\) and \(k=12\). In those cases \(2k+1\) is respectively \(9\) or \(25\), both composite, so the strengthened existence claim fails.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes not exceeding \(x\). For a positive integer \(n\) and an integer \(k\), the number of primes in
\[
((k-1)n,kn]
\]
is
\[
\pi(kn)-\pi((k-1)n),
\]
and the number of primes in the next interval \((kn,(k+1)n]\) is
\[
\pi((k+1)n)-\pi(kn).
\]
We disprove the strengthened assertion in the conjecture by taking
\[
n=14.
\]
This value satisfies \(14>1\) and \(14\ne 8\), so if the conjecture were true, there would have to be an integer \(k\) such that
\[
0<k<14,
\]
\(2k+1\) is prime, and
\[
\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1))
=
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k). \tag{1}
\]
We show that no such \(k\) exists.

For this purpose, divide the integers up to \(196=14\cdot14\) into consecutive blocks of length \(14\). The primes in these blocks, and hence their counts, are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
j&(14j,14(j+1)]&\text{primes in the interval}&c_j\\ \hline
0&(0,14]&2,3,5,7,11,13&6\\
1&(14,28]&17,19,23&3\\
2&(28,42]&29,31,37,41&4\\
3&(42,56]&43,47,53&3\\
4&(56,70]&59,61,67&3\\
5&(70,84]&71,73,79,83&4\\
6&(84,98]&89,97&2\\
7&(98,112]&101,103,107,109&4\\
8&(112,126]&113&1\\
9&(126,140]&127,131,137,139&4\\
10&(140,154]&149,151&2\\
11&(154,168]&157,163,167&3\\
12&(168,182]&173,179,181&3\\
13&(182,196]&191,193&2
\end{array}
\]
Here \(c_j\) denotes the number of primes in \((14j,14(j+1)]\). This table can be obtained by the elementary sieve of Eratosthenes. Indeed, every composite integer at most \(196\) has a prime divisor at most
\(\sqrt{196}=14\), so after retaining the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) themselves and removing the other multiples of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), precisely the displayed integers remain. Thus the table gives an exhaustive list, not merely a list of some primes in each interval. Also, every positive endpoint \(14j\) occurring here is composite, so the same counts would result if the interval endpoints were written open rather than half-open.

Equivalently, the prime-counting values at the block endpoints are obtained by taking cumulative sums:
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr}
x&0&14&28&42&56&70&84&98&112&126&140&154&168&182&196\\ \hline
\pi(x)&0&6&9&13&16&19&23&25&29&30&34&36&39&42&44.
\end{array}
\]
In particular,
\[
c_j=\pi(14(j+1))-\pi(14j).
\]
For a candidate \(k\) in (1), the left side of (1) is \(c_{k-1}\), while the right side is \(c_k\). Since \(0<k<14\), the only possible values are
\[
k=1,2,\ldots,13.
\]
Using the block counts above gives the complete case analysis
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
k&2k+1&c_{k-1}&c_k&c_{k-1}=c_k?\\ \hline
1&3&6&3&\text{no}\\
2&5&3&4&\text{no}\\
3&7&4&3&\text{no}\\
4&9&3&3&\text{yes}\\
5&11&3&4&\text{no}\\
6&13&4&2&\text{no}\\
7&15&2&4&\text{no}\\
8&17&4&1&\text{no}\\
9&19&1&4&\text{no}\\
10&21&4&2&\text{no}\\
11&23&2&3&\text{no}\\
12&25&3&3&\text{yes}\\
13&27&3&2&\text{no}.
\end{array}
\]
Thus equation (1) fails immediately in every case except \(k=4\) and \(k=12\). In the first exceptional case,
\[
2k+1=2\cdot4+1=9=3^2,
\]
which is not prime. In the second exceptional case,
\[
2k+1=2\cdot12+1=25=5^2,
\]
which is also not prime. Consequently, every integer \(k\) with \(0<k<14\) fails at least one of the two required conditions: for \(k\notin\{4,12\}\), the adjacent intervals contain different numbers of primes, while for \(k\in\{4,12\}\), the number \(2k+1\) is composite.

Therefore, for \(n=14\), there is no positive integer \(k<14\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime and the two adjacent intervals \(((k-1)14,14k]\) and \((14k,14(k+1)]\) have equal prime counts. Since \(14>1\) and \(14\ne8\), this directly contradicts the conjecture's “moreover” clause.

The conjecture is stated as a universal conjunction: for every \(n\), it asserts both the positivity condition for \(a(n)\) and this strengthened existence condition when \(n>1\) and \(n\ne8\). A conjunction is false as soon as one of its clauses is false. Hence it is unnecessary to decide the positivity assertion at \(n=14\): the failure of the strengthened existence assertion at \(n=14\) already disproves the full conjecture.
